steps.body: Real decisions rely on sampling every day — companies test products, cities plan services, schools check preferences. All of it starts with a random, representative sample.

predict.prompt: 2 defects in a sample of 50 phones. The factory made 5000 — a hundred times as many. Will the estimated defect count be small or large?

options.label: Large in count, small in rate — about 200

predict.reveal: A rare rate can still be a big count once the population is large. 2 in 50 is 4%, and 4% of 5000 is 200 — the RATE stayed tiny while the count grew a hundredfold.

widget.prompt: The sample is 2 defects out of 50 phones. Fill in the row for all 5000 phones, keeping the ratio the same.
widget.successFeedback: 200. The rate held at 2 in every 50 — 4% — all the way down the column, but a hundredfold bigger population turns a rare defect into 200 phones. Rate and count are different questions, and a sample answers the first in order to estimate the second.
widget.lowFeedback: Too low. Each 50 phones brings about 2 defects, and 5000 holds a hundred of those groups — count them up.
widget.highFeedback: Too high. Only 2 in every 50 are defective, so even 5000 phones cannot reach past 200.

explanationVariants: Randomly selecting from ALL customers avoids favoring any one group.
Surveying only satisfied customers who left reviews skews the result.

widget.prompt: A company wants to know overall customer satisfaction. Which method is LEAST biased?

options.label: Randomly call 300 customers from the full purchase records
options.feedback: Yes — a random call list from all customers avoids bias.

options.label: Read the reviews customers chose to post online
options.feedback: People who post reviews tend to have unusually strong (positive or negative) opinions — biased.

options.label: Survey people calling in with complaints
options.feedback: Complaint callers are, by definition, unhappy customers — a heavily biased group.

steps.body: A sample estimate is a best guess, not a guarantee — it can still differ from the true number, especially with a smaller sample.

widget.prompt: In a sample of 100 voters, 55 support a new law. If the district has 8000 voters, estimate how many support it.

commonErrors.feedback: That's just the sample count. Scale it up: 55/100 of 8000 = 4400.
That's every voter, not just supporters. Scale the ratio: 4400.

steps.body: The full sampling process: choose a random method, collect the sample, scale the ratio, and stay aware that a bigger sample builds more confidence.

widget.prompt: Which random sample gives a more reliable estimate of a city's average household income?

options.label: A random sample of 1000 households
options.feedback: Yes — a bigger random sample gives a more reliable estimate.

options.label: A random sample of 12 households
options.feedback: Too small — a sample this size can swing widely by chance.

options.label: Both are equally reliable
options.feedback: Sample size matters — the bigger one is more reliable.

explanationVariants: Scale the sample's ratio up to the full population.

widget.prompt: In a sample of 60 batteries, 3 fail early. If the factory made 6000 batteries, estimate how many fail early.

commonErrors.feedback: That's just the sample count. Scale it up: 3/60 of 6000 = 300.
That's all the batteries, not just failures. Scale the ratio: 300.

explanationVariants: A random draw from the full student list avoids bias.
Asking only students in one class or club skews the result.

widget.prompt: A school wants to know how students get to school. Which method is LEAST biased?

options.label: Randomly select 100 students from the whole school roster
options.feedback: Yes — a random draw from the full roster avoids bias.

options.label: Ask students waiting at the bus stop
options.feedback: Bus-stop students obviously ride the bus — heavily biased toward that answer.

options.label: Ask students in the school parking lot
options.feedback: Parking-lot students are biased toward driving or being driven — not representative.

explanationVariants: Scale the sample's ratio up to the full population.

widget.prompt: In a sample of 70 concertgoers, 35 bought a T-shirt. If 4200 people attended, estimate how many bought a T-shirt.

commonErrors.feedback: That's just the sample count. Scale it up: 35/70 of 4200 = 2100.
That's everyone, not just T-shirt buyers. Scale the ratio: 2100.

hints: Find the sample's ratio: 35 out of 70 = 1/2.
Apply that same ratio to 4200: 1/2 of 4200.

steps.body: Real sampling decisions combine three ideas: scale the ratio, keep the sample random, and trust bigger samples more.
takeaways: Scaling a sample's ratio works the same in any real-world context.
Always check whether a sample was truly random or secretly biased.
Bigger random samples give more confidence in the estimate.

concept.body: Scale a sample's ratio up to the full population in any real-world context: (trait count ÷ sample size) × population size.

concept.body: A random sample drawn from the whole population avoids bias. Sampling only from a convenient or self-selected group (reviewers, complainers, people already present) skews the result.
